mcqs.q: The three types of intra-oral radiograph are:
mcqs.explain: Intra-oral films are placed inside the mouth: periapical (IOPA), bitewing and occlusal.

mcqs.q: In 'periapical', the prefix peri- and root apical mean:
mcqs.explain: Peri = around, apical = apex; an IOPA shows the whole tooth and the bone around the root apex.

mcqs.q: A quality periapical radiograph should show at least:
opts: 2 mm of periapical bone with the complete root
mcqs.explain: It should record the complete area with the complete root and at least 2 mm of periapical bone, with minimal distortion and optimal density/contrast.

mcqs.q: The bisecting-angle technique is based on:
mcqs.explain: Cieszynski's rule of isometry: two triangles are equal when they share one complete side and have two equal angles — the basis of the bisecting (short-cone) technique.

mcqs.q: In the bisecting technique, the central ray is directed:
opts: Perpendicular to the imaginary bisector of the tooth-long-axis/film angle
Parallel to the long axis of the tooth
Through the apex of the root
mcqs.explain: The central ray is aimed perpendicular to the imaginary line bisecting the angle between the tooth's long axis and the film.

mcqs.q: Too MUCH vertical angulation in the bisecting technique produces:
mcqs.explain: Excess vertical angulation foreshortens the image; too little vertical angulation elongates it.

mcqs.q: The horizontal angulation for a periapical radiograph should be:
opts: 0° — the central ray passes through the contact areas
mcqs.explain: Horizontal angulation is always 0° (ray through the contacts, PID parallel to the labial/buccal surface); only the vertical angle changes per tooth.

mcqs.q: The correct vertical angulation for a MAXILLARY canine (bisecting) is about:
mcqs.explain: Maxillary verticals: incisors +40°, canines +45°, premolars +30°, molars +20°.

mcqs.q: The correct vertical angulation for a MANDIBULAR molar (bisecting) is about:
mcqs.explain: Mandibular verticals: incisors −15°, canines −20°, premolars −10°, molars −5°.

mcqs.q: In the paralleling (long-cone) technique:
opts: The film is parallel to the long axis and the central ray is perpendicular to both
The ray bisects the angle between film and tooth
The film touches the tooth surface
A short cone is always used
mcqs.explain: In paralleling, the film is held parallel to the tooth's long axis (with a holder) and the central ray strikes both at right angles, using a long FSFD.

mcqs.q: Compared with bisecting, the paralleling technique is preferred because it gives:
opts: The least dimensional distortion and is reproducible
No need for a film holder
mcqs.explain: Paralleling produces the most geometrically accurate, least-distorted, reproducible image — the recommended IOPA technique.

mcqs.q: A bitewing radiograph is described as intra-oral but NOT periapical because:
opts: It does not show the root apex
It is taken outside the mouth
mcqs.explain: A bitewing shows the crowns of both arches and crestal bone but not the apices, so it is not a periapical view.

mcqs.q: The PRIMARY indication for a bitewing radiograph is detecting:
opts: Interproximal (incipient) caries and crestal bone loss
mcqs.explain: Bitewings are best for interproximal/incipient caries, caries progression, restorations, early bone loss and calculus.

mcqs.q: The vertical angulation used for a bitewing radiograph is about:
mcqs.explain: A bitewing uses ~+10° vertical angulation, with the horizontal ray passing through the contacts.

mcqs.q: A bitewing is contraindicated / unhelpful when you need to assess:
mcqs.explain: Because radicular and periradicular structures are not shown, a bitewing cannot evaluate periapical pathology.

mcqs.q: A radiograph cannot show the bucco-lingual position of an object because it is:
mcqs.explain: The image is a 2D projection of a 3D object, so depth (bucco-lingual relationship) is lost — hence localization techniques are needed.

mcqs.q: The parallax (tube-shift) localization method is also known as:
mcqs.explain: Parallax (Clark, 1909) is the tube-shift technique, summarised by the SLOB rule (Clark's rule).

mcqs.q: SLOB stands for:
mcqs.explain: SLOB = Same Lingual, Opposite Buccal — describes how the object shifts relative to the tube movement.

mcqs.q: Using the SLOB rule, if an object moves in the SAME direction as the tube shift, it lies:
opts: In the same plane as the reference
mcqs.explain: An object that moves the same way as the tube is lingual (Same Lingual); one moving opposite is buccal (Opposite Buccal).

mcqs.q: The right-angle localization technique combines:
opts: An occlusal and a periapical radiograph (beams ~90° apart)
A panoramic and a lateral ceph
mcqs.explain: The right-angle technique takes a periapical and an occlusal view whose beams are at 90°, giving two perpendicular planes.

mcqs.q: Which is a recognised indication for OCCLUSAL radiography?
opts: Assessing the extent of cysts/tumours and detecting sialoliths
mcqs.explain: Occlusal films show the size/extent of cysts and tumours, fractures, sialoliths, foreign bodies and unerupted teeth, and help patients with trismus.

mcqs.q: The vertical angulation for a true (cross-sectional) MAXILLARY occlusal view is about:
mcqs.explain: Maxillary occlusal: true/cross-sectional +65°, anterior +45°, lateral +60°, vertex +90°.

mcqs.q: A cross-sectional MANDIBULAR occlusal radiograph is taken at about:
opts: −90° (beam at right angles to the film)
mcqs.explain: The cross-sectional mandibular occlusal uses −90° (true occlusal), giving a bucco-lingual view of the mandible.

mcqs.q: A full-mouth radiographic survey conventionally consists of:
mcqs.explain: A classic full-mouth series is 21 films: 17 IOPAs plus 4 bitewings.

saqs.q: List the criteria of a quality periapical radiograph.
saqs.a: Complete area with complete root, at least 2 mm periapical bone, least geometric distortion, and optimal density & contrast.

saqs.q: State Cieszynski's rule of isometry and how it applies to the bisecting technique.
saqs.a: Two triangles are equal when they share one complete side and two equal angles. The ray is aimed perpendicular to the bisector of the angle between the tooth's long axis and the film, so the image length equals the true tooth length.

saqs.q: Compare the bisecting and paralleling techniques.
saqs.a: Bisecting (short cone): ray ⊥ bisector, more distortion, no holder needed. Paralleling (long cone): film parallel to long axis, ray ⊥ both, least distortion, reproducible — preferred.

saqs.q: Give the indications and main limitation of bitewing radiography.
saqs.a: Indications: interproximal/incipient caries & progression, restorations, early bone loss, calculus. Limitation: roots/apices not shown — cannot assess periapical pathology.

saqs.q: Explain the SLOB rule for object localization.
saqs.a: Same Lingual, Opposite Buccal. Take 2 films with a tube shift: if the object moves the same direction as the tube it is lingual; if opposite, it is buccal (reference = adjacent root).

saqs.q: List four indications for occlusal radiography.
saqs.a: Extent of cysts/tumours, fractures of alveolus, sialoliths, foreign bodies, unerupted/impacted teeth, and patients with trismus.

saqs.q: Why are object-localization techniques needed, and name the two methods.
saqs.a: Because a radiograph is a 2D image of a 3D object (no bucco-lingual depth). Methods: parallax (tube-shift/SLOB) and the right-angle technique.
